record.title: Miller Interview with Pham Xuan An

point.title: The Rivalry Between Ngô Đình Nhu and Ngô Đình Cẩn
point.partial_transcript: Nayan Chanda, whom I think you knew very well.
point.synopsis: After a brief discussion about Edward Miller's advisor, professor Hồ Huệ Tâm, PXA discusses the relationship between the Ngô brothers, stating that the perceived rivalry between the intellectual Ngô Đình Nhu and the less-educated Ngô Đình Cẩn was not real. He explains it was an appearance they maintained to gather intelligence on their subordinates. PXA describes Ngô Đình Cẩn as a smart, powerful grassroots operator who worked underground before 1954 to build a constituency in Huế. He states that Cẩn supplied the Diệm regime with key personnel, including men who worked for Nhu, and secretly invested in Buddhist institutions to build influence.
point.keywords: Ngô Đình Diệm; Ngô Đình Nhu; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngô Đình Thục; Rivalry; Grassroots; Huế; Ngo Dinh Diem; Ngo Dinh Nhu; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngo Dinh Thuc; Hue; Ngo Family Dynamics; Hồ Huệ Tâm

point.title: Labor Unions
point.partial_transcript: What about Trần Quốc Bửu and the Vietnamese Confederation of Labor?
point.synopsis: PXA discusses Trần Quốc Bửu's journey as a politically flexible figure shaped by overlapping foreign influences in Vietnam during the mid-20th century. He initially worked with the Việt Minh and received Japanese training alongside leaders like Nguyễn Bình and Trình Minh Thế. Later, French intelligence recruited him to lead anti-communist labor organizations, countering worker mobilization by communists. In the early 1950s, he cooperated with Ngô Đình Diệm and joined the Cần Lao party under Ngô Đình Nhu’s influence. Despite these alliances with both French and South Vietnamese authorities, his relationship with Diệm’s regime ultimately proved short-lived and unstable.
point.keywords: Trần Quốc Bửu; Labor Unions; French G2; Japanese; Catholic Church; Labor Movements in Vietnam; Anti-communism; Tran Quoc Buu; Catholic Federation of Workers; Ngo Brothers

point.title: Dr. Trần Kim Tuyến's Role in 1950s South Vietnamese Politics
point.synopsis: In 1955–56, Ngô Đình Diệm intensified authoritarian control by abolishing traditional village elections and suppressing opposition, including nationalist and religious groups like the Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo, despite their anti-communist stance. This caused widespread dissatisfaction and strikes, particularly among villagers. At the same time, Dr. Trần Kim Tuyến, a trusted political operative under Ngô Đình Diệm, led the Political, Social, and Cultural Office, which included secret police functions despite his limited formal intelligence training. To prevent communist influence, he deliberately split up the Office as well as made a new labor organization, ensuring mutual surveillance and control. The office had previously been headed by Vũ Tiến Huân, a French-trained administrator and Diệm ally. By late 1956, Tuyến replaced Huân as chief of the Office, following reorganizations. PXA then shifted to discuss Dr. Tuyến's background. He is someone who is more to the Catholic Church than personally to the Ngô family, with a background in religion and literature as well as partial medical education disrupted by French military conscription.
point.keywords: Trần Kim Tuyến; Tran Kim Tuyen; Ngô Đình Diệm; Ngo Dinh Diem; Vũ Tiến Huân; Vu Tien Huan; Anti-communism; political manuevers; Political, Social, and Cultural Office; 1956; Catholic; Dr. Tuyen's background; Ngo brothers

point.title: Lê Khắc Duyệt's Role in 1950s South Vietnamese Politics
point.partial_transcript: Yes. I read about that in, AJ Langguth's book.
point.synopsis: The speaker recounts returning from the United States (1957–59) and seeking employment through connections with Lê Khắc Duyệt, the Chief of Police and Security of Central Vietnam under Ngô Đình Cẩn. He describes a period of intense repression in which a large proportion of suspected cadres in Cochinchina were arrested or killed, attributing primary responsibility to Cẩn rather than other officials. These actions allegedly included extralegal detention and transfers to Huế. Duyệt is portrayed as a loyal, due to his French training, non-political administrator who exercised restraint, sometimes delaying harsh orders, and retained Cẩn’s trust despite internal religious and political pressures.
point.keywords: Lê Khắc Duyệt; Le Khac Duyet; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngo Dinh Can

point.title: The 1960 Coup Attempt and Ngô Đình Cẩn's Foresight
point.partial_transcript: But here, they look down upon him in Saigon.
point.synopsis: PXA recounts the November 1960 coup attempt and the contempt intellectuals held for Ngô Đình Cẩn despite his foreknowledge. Cẩn sent a detailed warning to Ngô Đình Nhu, who dismissed it due to condescension. This led PXA to meet Cẩn in Huế to understand his intelligence methods. Cẩn used a counterinsurgency strategy involving arresting suspected communist agents, detaining them extralegally, then releasing some as covert informants to monitor nationalist opposition, which is seen as a more immediate threat. This network enabled the regime to track political activity and anticipate coups. Cẩn also commanded respect from subordinates, including Tôn Thất Đính, defending him against the disdain the urban intellectuals had for Cẩn .
point.keywords: 1960 Coup; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngô Đình Nhu; Intelligence Report; Dr. Tuyến; Elbridge Durbrow; Ngo Dinh Can; Vietcong; VC; VNQDD; Tôn Thất Đính; Ton That Dinh; Disregard; intelligence; nationalist opposition; counterinsurgency; Anti-communism

point.title: Ngô Đình Cẩn and the Ngô Brothers' Dynamics in the 1950s
point.partial_transcript: And he was–he seems to have been less Catholic than his brothers,
point.synopsis: The passage portrays Ngô Đình Cẩn as a pragmatic operator who built support beyond Catholic networks, unlike some of his family members. It highlights connections between Ngô Đình Thục and international Catholic figures such as Francis Spellman, alongside claims of broader political and intelligence ties with America during the anti-French war. It also suggests coordination rather than rivalry between Cẩn, Ngô Đình Nhu, and Ngô Đình Diệm, using overlapping reporting networks to monitor subordinates. PXA also remarks how Cẩn is smarter than Nhu and Thục due to his ability to discern flatterers.
point.keywords: Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngo Dinh Thuc; Ngô Đình Thục; anti-French; Catholic collaboration; Vatican involvement; Francis Spellman; Ngo Brothers

point.title: The Regime's Decline
point.partial_transcript: And if that was the case, why did it change after the 1950’s?
point.synopsis: PXA discusses why the Diệm regime ultimately failed and the Communist party made a comeback. He states the regime had no real constituency and alienated key segments of the population. He describes how the regime dispossessed peasants of their land through the Agroville and Strategic Hamlet programs, abolished traditional village elections in 1956, and forced Chinese residents to take Vietnamese citizenship, creating widespread animosity. PXA explains that this drove many patriots and intellectuals to support the Việt Minh.
point.keywords: Agroville; Strategic Hamlet; Land confiscation; Nationalism; Opposition; Việt Minh; Vietnamese Rural Politics; Viet Minh; Chinese businessmen; animosity

point.title: Bến Cát Intelligence Operation
point.partial_transcript: So Ngô Ðình Cẩn, I went there. See, I give you some anecdote, many anecdote. He like a cow, with a cow milk.
point.synopsis: PXA discusses an intelligence operation run from a dairy farm in Bến Cát. He describes the farm as being run by an Australian air force veteran and established near a communist military zone to recruit local workers and train them as intelligence assets for the South Vietnamese, American, and Australian governments. He also recounts an incident in November 1961 where an Egyptian involved with the farm was kidnapped by local guerrillas, stating the motive was simply to acquire stationery, a typewriter, and paper. Ngô Đình Cẩn’s fondness for animals led subordinates to present gifts like cows and trained dogs from the Bến Cát farm as acts of flattery. PXA highlights how aides exploited minor details to discredit rivals like Phạm Quốc Thuần as well as Cẩn’s role in recruiting loyal personnel, including individuals sent to the United States for training and later integrated into the regime.
point.keywords: Bến Cát; Dairy Farm; Espionage; CIA; Australia; Kidnapping; Ben Cat; Intelligence Operations; Australian Involvement in Vietnam; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngo Dinh Can; communists; Phạm Quốc Thuần; Pham Quoc Thuan; sycophants

point.title: The 1963 Buddhist Crisis
point.partial_transcript: Okay. I'm sure––I think we should probably finish up here because I know you've not been feeling well. Let me ask you one more question, though, about the Buddhist movement in 1963, Phong trào Phật giáo.
point.synopsis: PXA describes the 1963 Buddhist movement in Huế as primarily a reaction against Ngô Đình Thục’s religious policies, while noting that Ngô Đình Cẩn initially maintained cooperative relations with Buddhists but followed Thục’s authority in key decisions and aggravations against the Buddhists. He links the unrest to both local grievances, including restrictions on religious expression and the May 1963 Huế incident, and to a longer-term international Buddhist movement for unity. Figures such as Thích Trí Quang are presented as influential organizers, with connections to earlier political and intelligence networks and involvement in protest actions like the self-immolation of Thích Quảng Đức. The account further claims that U.S. actors, including the Central Intelligence Agency, monitored the situation, anticipated unrest, and maintained contacts with Buddhist figures. It also alleges that intelligence files on Trí Quang were destroyed and that he was later positioned in regional Buddhist activities, while journalists and informants were encouraged to closely track Buddhist developments in Huế leading up to the crisis.
point.keywords: Ngô Đình Thục; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Catholic Church; Huế; Religious Conflict in Vietnam; 1963 Buddhist Crisis; Ngo Dinh Thuc; Ngo Dinh Can; Thích Trí Quang; Thich Tri Quang; buddhist activism; CIA

point.title: Ngô Đình Cẩn's Trial and Death
point.partial_transcript: Before May, the signs were already there?
point.synopsis: PXA discusses the trial and execution of Ngô Đình Cẩn following the 1963 coup. He states that Cẩn was tried by a military court under Nguyễn Khánh's government in 1964 for illegal actions against civilians. He describes how Cẩn smartly denied having any official power during the trial. PXA asserts that Cẩn was ultimately sentenced to death because he refused to give several million dollars from a Swiss bank account to General Khánh, choosing to give it to the Catholic Church instead. He states his belief that Cẩn would have been released if he had given the money to Khánh.
point.keywords: Ngô Đình Cẩn; Trial; Nguyễn Khánh; Dương Văn Hiếu; Military Court; post-coup South Vietnam; 1964; Political trials

00:13:31.990 --> 00:13:43.621 <v PXA> Oh yeah! And that one had a representative here. The first representative is Mr. <c.124>Trần Khánh Vân</c>.
00:13:43.621 --> 00:13:45.000 <v Edward Miller> <c.125>Trần Khánh Vân</c>?
00:13:45.000 --> 00:14:01.299 <v PXA> Yeah, I don’t know whether he died or not, but he is a bit older then I. He should be born in <c.126>1923</c>, <c.127>‘24</c>. His office is near the <c.128>Thanh Niên Restaurant</c>.
00:14:01.299 --> 00:14:16.500 <v Edward Miller> Oh, really? Okay. So <c.129>Bửu</c>, by the early fifties, is working with the Ngô brothers but with the French as well, you're saying?
00:14:16.500 --> 00:14:29.618 <v PXA> Yeah, and when <c.130>Ngô Ðình <c.131>Diệm</c></c> came to power, he was recruited by Diệm, too, particularly by Dr. <c.132>Tuyến</c>, et cetera. So he was made member of the <c.133>Cần Lao party</c>.
00:14:29.618 --> 00:14:31.519 <v Edward Miller> At that time?
00:14:31.519 --> 00:14:33.011 <v PXA> At that time.
00:14:33.011 --> 00:14:36.950 <v Edward Miller> But the relationship doesn’t last very long.
00:14:36.950 --> 00:14:40.460 <v PXA> No, he doesn’t last long.
00:14:40.460 --> 00:14:47.620 <v Edward Miller> And what was the source of the break, did it have to do with the strikes in <c.134>1956</c>?
00:14:47.620 --> 00:15:25.000 <v PXA> <c.135><c.136>1956</c></c>, 1955, 1956? Yeah, there was a strike <c.137>'56</c>. This was because after <c.138>Diệm</c> used the dictatorial policy, he controlled everything and he dissolved the village election, the traditional one. But, according to the Vietnamese, “Lệ vua thua lệ làng.”
00:15:25.000 --> 00:15:29.847 <v Edward Miller> The writ of the emperor stops at the village gate.
00:15:29.847 --> 00:16:38.009 <v PXA> So the Vietnamese were very upset about that, the villagers particularly. So he set up his own way. So in <c.139>‘56</c>, when he was sure that he had the support of Americans to consolidate his family power. Even the opposition, the legal opposition—like <c.140>Đại Việt</c>, V.N.Q.D.D., the <c.141>Hòa Hảo</c>, the <c.142>Cao Đài</c>, et cetera—all of them were anti-<c.143>Việt Minh</c>, or anti-Communist for sure. Many of them cooperated with Việt Minh for a while at the beginning, because all of them were patriotic people. So, <c.144>Diệm</c> didn’t want them to be opposition in the government, so he considered them––outlawed all of them. Cao, Thiên, Hòa, Bình. All of them were outlawed. Cao means <c.145>Cao Đài</c>. Thiên, <c.146><c.147>Thiên Chúa Giáo</c></c>, Thiên Chúa Giáo in the South. And Hòa, <c.148>Hòa Hảo</c>. Bình, <c.149>Bình Xuyên</c>.
00:16:38.009 --> 00:16:44.250 <v Edward Miller> But what about <c.150>Bửu</c> and his unions? Where–
00:16:44.250 --> 00:17:29.130 <v PXA> So he continued to work. And Dr. <c.151><c.152>Tuyến</c></c> is smart––he divided––Dr. Tuyến is in charge of, the Chief of the Political and Social–Chính trị Xã hội–and Cultural Office. That includes also the secret police, too. He's not a professional intelligence officer now. But he's a man trusted by the <c.153>Catholic Church</c> to run the show, particularly in politics. And not intelligence, et cetera. He learned it later from the British and then from the American <c.154>CIA</c>.
00:17:29.130 --> 00:17:32.000 <v Edward Miller> So what was his––
00:17:32.000 --> 00:17:38.210 <v PXA> <c.155><c.156>Tuyến</c></c> [inaudible]. At the same time, Tuyến set up another labor organization.
00:17:38.210 --> 00:17:41.000 <v Edward Miller> I see. What was it called?
00:17:41.000 --> 00:17:42.000 <v PXA> <c.157>Lực lượng Lao động</c>.
00:17:42.000 --> 00:17:45.000 <v Edward Miller> <c.158>Lực lượng Lao động</c>?
00:17:45.000 --> 00:18:12.609 <v PXA> No no, not <c.159>Lực lượng Lao động</c>. By his own man. I asked him why he did it. He said very simple. If you have only one Federation, in case it gets infiltrated by the communists, they go on strike and we would be in a very bad position. So we should divide them. We have two of them to compete in order to counterbalance.
00:18:12.609 --> 00:18:15.369 <v Edward Miller> And when did he do that? Do you remember?
00:18:15.369 --> 00:18:23.849 <v PXA> Uh, he did that when he took over that office. That office was first run by, uh.
00:18:23.849 --> 00:18:25.930 <v Edward Miller> [inaudible]
00:18:25.930 --> 00:18:35.720 <v PXA> Sở Nghiên cứu Chính trị Xã Hội và Văn hoá––that office was first run by Mr. <c.160>Vũ Tiến Huân</c>.
00:18:35.720 --> 00:18:36.000 <v Edward Miller> I'm sorry. What's his name?
00:18:36.000 --> 00:18:41.000 <v PXA> <c.161>Vũ Tiến Huân</c>. H-U-A-N.
00:18:41.000 --> 00:19:34.839 <v PXA> <c.162>Vũ Tiến Huân</c> was a mandarin; he was Đốc phủ sứ. Only two North Vietnamese were made <c.163>Đốc phủ sứ in th</c>e South. One is <c.164>Trịnh Đình Thảo</c>, who had a law degree. This one has administrative degree in <c.165><c.167>Hanoi</c></c>. That course was reserved for––even <c.166>Ngô Đình Diệm</c>––took that course in Hanoi. Administration school. But the <c.168>South</c>, because of colony, so the highest rank for them was the district Chief, not province Chief. But for <c.169>Protectorate</c>, they were made province Chief like <c.170>Ngô Đình Diệm</c> and the others. So that man––I had a mental block––I just mentioned––
00:19:34.839 --> 00:19:37.599 <v Edward Miller> <c.171>Trịnh Đình Thảo</c>? Or––
00:19:37.599 --> 00:19:52.799 <v PXA> <c.172>Trịnh Đình Thảo</c> and the other one is <c.173><c.174>Vũ Tiến Huân</c></c>. Vũ Tiến Huân, when the French returned, he was made Chief of <c.175><c.176><c.177>Chợ Lớn</c></c></c> province. At that time, Chợ Lớn became a province. Under the French, Chợ Lớn is a province.
00:19:52.799 --> 00:19:55.880 <v Edward Miller> In <c.178>1945</c> this was?
00:19:55.880 --> 00:20:20.000 <v PXA> Before <c.179>'45</c>, <c.180>Chợ Lớn</c> is a province, <c.181>Gia Định</c> not a province. Now both of them merged together to make <c.182>Hồ Chí Minh City</c>. Then <c.183>Chợ Lớn</c> has their own mayor, and <c.184>Saigon</c> their own mayor too. Then <c.185>Vũ Tiến Huân</c> was made by the French, when the French returned, the province Chief of <c.186>Chợ Lớn</c>.
00:20:20.000 --> 00:20:21.000 <v Edward Miller> <c.187>Chợ Lớn</c>.
00:20:21.000 --> 00:20:51.240 <v PXA> And <c.188>Ngô Đình Thục</c>'s family, particularly <c.189>Ngô Đình Diệm</c>, when he returned from Europe or from the <c.190>U.S.</c> or from <c.191>Japan</c>, he went to his friend in <c.192>Chợ Lớn</c>. That's why he became a good friend of <c.193><c.194>Vũ Tiến Huân</c></c>. Vũ Tiến Huân protects these people. So that's why when he came to power, he made him head of that one, but he's not Catholic.
00:20:51.240 --> 00:20:52.440 <v Edward Miller> <c.195>Huân</c> was not Catholic?
00:20:52.440 --> 00:20:59.519 <v PXA> Huân was not Catholic. He's a good friend of my father. I know him very well. He liked<c.196> th</c>e movie, he liked pictures, et cetera.
00:20:59.519 --> 00:21:16.759 <v PXA> He was in <c.197>Gia Định</c> before, and he was made chief of that one. But after that and the reorganization, they used their trusted man, so <c.198>Tuyến</c> was made head of that one in 19––late <c.199>'56</c>.
00:21:16.759 --> 00:21:26.599 <c.201> to N<c.202>hu</c</c>>?<c.203></c>
00:21:26.599 --> 00:21:30.549 <v PXA> No, he close to the church.
00:21:30.549 --> 00:21:35.230 <v Edward Miller> The church. So <c.204>Thục</c>? Was he recruited by <c.205>Ngô Đình Thục</c>?
00:21:35.230 --> 00:21:36.509 <v PXA> No, by the church.
00:21:36.509 --> 00:21:38.000 <v Edward Miller> By the church?
00:21:38.000 --> 00:21:40.849 <v PXA> Bùi Chu, <c.206>Phát Diệm</c>, <c.207>or someplac</c>e.
00:21:40.849 --> 00:21:41.950 <v Edward Miller> Was he from the North?
00:21:41.950 --> 00:21:43.000 <v PXA> Yeah. He from <c.208>Thanh Hoá</c>.
00:21:43.000 --> 00:21:46.869 <v Edward Miller> <c.209>Thanh Hoá</c>? I see.
00:21:46.869 --> 00:22:13.000 <v PXA> He intended to be the Catholic priest. He attended the seminars. But then he learned, after that, he got the degree of Literature––Cử nhân Văn chương. After that, he took another course called the medical school.
00:22:13.000 --> 00:22:14.081 <v Edward Miller> In <c.210>Hanoi</c>?
00:22:14.081 --> 00:22:32.470 <v PXA> In <c.211>Hanoi</c>. And then where he met the midwife who became later his wife. He was in love with that midwife, so he quit being a seminarist and married this lady and became a doctor.
00:22:32.470 --> 00:22:57.000 <v PXA> But doctor without thesis. Do you know why? Because he was drafted into the army. So those who go to medical school, they are authorized to go there to attend the first five years. After the sixth year, you prepare your thesis, and then after graduation, at the seventh year, you got the Doctor degree.
00:22:57.000 --> 00:23:30.710 <v PXA> But the French were very smart. They drafted at the end of the fifth year and to serve the army as a medical doctor. But when they were dismissed or they were demobilized, they weren't allowed to write the thesis that they experienced during the war––to write the thesis and to get the doctorate degree. We had many doctors without thesis, so they cannot practice their profession, like Dr. <c.212>Tuyến</c> and Dr. <c.213>Đàm Quang Trung</c>, et cetera.
00:23:30.710 --> 00:23:35.750 <v Edward Miller> I see because they had been drafted into the army before they wrote the thesis and then afterwards they didn't––
00:23:35.750 --> 00:23:54.349 <v PXA> Afterwards, they were not––they could not open the cabinet, the medical cabinet. You are a doctor, but you don't know how to to give a shot to the people. I can do it better than you. He's a good friend of mine.
00:23:54.349 --> 00:24:04.000 <v Edward Miller> Yes. I read about that in, <c.214>AJ Langguth</c>'s book.<c.215></c>
00:24:04.000 --> 00:24:14.109 <v PXA> He helped me a lot when I applied for the visa. Very difficult to get at that time. I had a lot of problems.
00:24:14.109 --> 00:24:15.990 <v Edward Miller> You mean to go to <c.216>the United States</c>?
00:24:15.990 --> 00:24:38.019 <v PXA> Yeah. Even when the American agree everything, but on the Vietnamese side, they were very tough. But then when I returned, I applied to work for him, and he agreed because I had a friend working for <c.217>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>. He's the chief of Police and Security of <c.218>Central Vietnam</c>.
00:24:38.019 --> 00:24:39.000 <v Edward Miller> Who was he?
00:24:39.000 --> 00:24:41.000 <v PXA> Mr. <c.219>Lê Khắc Duyệt</c>.
00:24:41.000 --> 00:24:42.500 <v Edward Miller><c.221> <c.220>Lê Kh</c>ắc Duyệt</c>?
00:24:42.500 --> 00:24:53.000 <v PXA> Yeah, he's a relative of <c.222>Lê Khắc Quyến</c>. Many Lê Khắc's joined the revolution in the <c.223>North</c>. That's a very well-known family in <c.224>Huế</c>.<c.225></c>
00:24:53.000 --> 00:24:57.460 <v Edward Miller> So you were in <c.226>the United States</c> at what time?
00:24:57.460 --> 00:25:03.019 <v PXA> <c.227>'57</c> to <c.228>'59</c>. I went there October 10th and returned October 8th.
00:25:03.019 --> 00:25:13.000 <v Edward Miller> So you you came back in in <c.229>1959</c>? And this Lê Khắc Duyệt helped you?
00:25:13.000 --> 00:25:37.000 <v PXA> I applied to work for him because I was not––because many of our people were already arrested. My boss too, Mr. Hương, et cetera. All of them in <c.230>1957</c> and <c.231>'58</c>. 85% of cadres left in <c.232>South</c> Vietnam were either arrested or killed, most of them killed.
00:25:37.000 --> 00:25:38.000 <v Edward Miller> 85%?
00:25:38.000 --> 00:25:56.740 <v PXA> 85% out of 60,000 left behind. Hardcores in <c.233>Cochinchina</c>. I don't know about <c.234>Central Vietnam</c> or High Plateau, but <c.235>Cochinchina</c>, that's important, because it includes <c.236>Chợ Lớn</c>, <c.237>Gia Định</c> et cetera–that's the headquarter.
00:25:56.740 --> 00:25:59.500 <v Edward Miller> So the policies were very effective?
00:25:59.500 --> 00:26:05.579 <v PXA> Very efficient, very efficient. <c.238>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> did it.
00:26:05.579 --> 00:26:07.769 <v Edward Miller> So <c.239>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>––
00:26:07.769 --> 00:26:12.180 <v PXA> <c.240><c.243>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c></c> did it, not <c.241>Ngô Đình Nhu</c> or Dr. <c.242>Tuyến</c>. No no no, Ngô Đình Cẩn did it.
00:26:12.180 --> 00:26:16.000 <v Edward Miller> Really? So even in <c.244>South Vietnam</c>, it was <c.245>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>––
00:26:16.000 --> 00:26:47.000 <v PXA> <c.246>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> who did that. He kidnapped them. He did not use the law, because to arrest the people, you should have the law, et cetera. The legacy of French administration: if you have a suspect, you can detain him; you call it preventive detention, but you cannot send him to jail. You see the point there? But for <c.247>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>, forget about that. You just kidnapped and took them to <c.248>Huế</c>.
00:26:47.000 --> 00:26:48.680 <v Edward Miller> To <c.249>Huế</c>?
00:26:48.680 --> 00:27:26.210 <v PXA> To <c.250>Huế</c>, there'd be all kind of underground prison, et cetera. They have here in [Tân Hội?] a place to keep these people that they kidnap in the street, and another place here on Lê Văn <c.251>Duyệt</c> Street. The two places, they kidnapped them and they took to <c.252>Huế</c>, under the protection of <c.253>Tuyến</c>, because he was Chief of police and everything. He oversees; he was not director.
00:27:26.210 --> 00:27:27.569 <v Edward Miller> This is [Lê Khắc Duyệt?]
00:27:27.569 --> 00:28:32.289 <v PXA> [Lê Khắc Duyệt?]. He was also a very nice man. He was functionaire under the French, and then he was made Chief police under the French. And <c.254>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> know him, know that he's very not naughty, and he's a good government cadre because he is from <c.255>Huế</c>, so he knows all the big families. So he used the man, he know that the man is very loyal to the regime––any regime. The French trained that way: if you are made functionaire, you'd just be loyal to the the system. You are not politician, so you have no problem. See it? So he know that. Good one. He's Buddhist probably too, but <c.256>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>––he's Catholic, et cetera. He's surrounded by a lot of Catholics. These Catholics, you know, used tricks to push <c.257>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> to get rid of this man.
00:28:32.289 --> 00:28:33.009 <v Edward Miller> Oh, really?
00:28:33.009 --> 00:28:59.130 <v PXA> Yeah. How are you to have the one Chief of police, he's a Buddhist? In the meantime, you are Catholic. Your parent, your father, et cetera, Catholic, et cetera. The regime is for the Catholic, but you have one Chief of Secret Police and Security and Police of <c.258>Central Vietnam</c>––a Buddhist. That is very dangerous.
00:28:59.130 --> 00:29:02.250 <v Edward Miller> When did that happen? When did <c.259>Cẩn</c> get rid of––?
00:29:02.250 --> 00:29:20.519 <v PXA> No, he didn't get rid of him. He did not get rid of this one. He yelled at the other one. He scolded them. He said, look, you people, you are a flatterer, troublemaker.
00:29:20.519 --> 00:29:23.519 <v Edward Miller> He's talking to his Catholic supporters?
00:29:23.519 --> 00:31:27.670 <v PXA> Yeah, the Catholic supporters. He scolded them. He said, look, I know this man. He's not naughty, he's very human. Even though if he see, you kill a chicken, if you cut the head of a chicken––the Vietnamese way of killing, not like American. He couldn't––he closed his eyes, and sometimes he fainted by looking at that. So he's very human. So I used him, and he loyal, he report everything to me that he knows. For instance, if I mad––I can get mad very easily, I have hot temper. If I heard something, I said alright, kill him. And if I tell it to you, you automatically kick him out and kill him. But Duyệt, when I tell him alright, this <c.260>VC</c> is very bad, kill him––but he dared not do it. He knows my temperament, he just keep it. He did not report that he kill or not, et cetera. One week later, I change my mind. I feel repent not by doing that, because that's too much, because that's suspected, not real, concrete. I said alright, have you killed that man yet? He said, not yet, because I know that you have hot temper. But if now you decide, I will kill. No, no, now I change my mind. Alright, let him leave. You see? If the other one is Catholic, automatically they are flatterer. He is so smart that way. But here, they look down upon him in <c.261><c.262>Saigon</c></c>. Saigon is intellectual, et cetera, than Central Vietnamese. But this is the Lý trưởng. Lý trưởng that means a village official––they call it Lý trưởng in <c.263>Central Vietnam</c>. And the youngest son of the family, Út trầu––they gave him all kind of titles. And he was stupid––
00:31:27.670 --> 00:31:28.950 <v Edward Miller> To?
00:31:28.950 --> 00:31:45.069 <v PXA> To <c.264>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>. The people in <c.265>Central Vietnam</c>, in <c.266>South Vietnam</c>, particularly intellectuals from <c.267>Hanoi</c> and intellectuals from <c.268>Saigon</c>, they considered <c.269>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> a stupid man, fool around, you know?
00:31:45.069 --> 00:31:48.190 <v Edward Miller> But in fact, they didn't appreciate how effective he was?
00:31:48.190 --> 00:32:07.000 <v PXA> They did not know, and they looked down upon him. And when the coup happened in <c.270>1960</c>––you know, the <c.271>November coup</c>. Actually the coup was orchestrated by <c.272>Durbrow</c>, <c.273>Elbridge Durbrow</c>, the ambassador.
00:32:07.000 --> 00:32:07.638 <v Edward Miller> <c.274>Durbrow</c>?
00:32:07.638 --> 00:33:27.509 <v PXA> He was official of the American embassy in Moscow. He was assigned here first when <c.275>Diệm</c> became president, et cetera. He replaced <c.276>Reinhardt</c>––<c.277><c.278>Frederick Reinhardt</c></c>, the ambassador. Frederick Reinhardt came here to replace the special envoy, General <c.279>Lawton Collins</c>. So when they pulled a coup, the coup failed, just to intimidate <c.280>Diệm</c>, to force him to reorganize his administration. Put pressure on him, that's all, but not to get rid of him yet. That's the first sign that Americans need to be involved here more, et cetera. That's a very long story. Yeah. So the coup was over. But before the coup happened, <c.281>Ngô Ðình Cẩn</c>, he sent here a telegram, a long report that a coup is going to happen against the regime in a very short time.
00:33:27.509 --> 00:33:29.430 <v Edward Miller> This was before the coup took place?
00:33:29.430 --> 00:33:39.794 <v PXA> Before the coup took place––Excuse me [coughing]. So and then I asked Dr. <c.282>Tuyến</c>, et cetera.
00:33:39.794 --> 00:33:41.910 <v Edward Miller> I'm sorry. You asked who?
00:33:41.910 --> 00:34:14.260 <v PXA> He sent a report to <c.283>Ngô Ðình Nhu</c>, to inform him in advance that the coup is going to happen. But <c.284>Ngô Ðình Nhu</c> looked down upon his young brother–– not only his young brother, but he was not intellectual. He didn't know much. You know. And he sent over. And how could he know the situation in <c.285>Saigon</c>? You see? So. And he checked in the waste bucket. But the other one. Pick it up. They are not to burn it.
00:34:14.260 --> 00:34:16.619 <v Edward Miller> Who picked it up?
00:34:16.619 --> 00:34:22.980 <v PXA> The man of of <c.286>Ngo Dinh Nhu</c> [inaudible] the pick up in order not to burn it. But nobody knew. He was so mad.
00:34:22.980 --> 00:34:23.980 <v Edward Miller> Just. Right. Right.
00:34:23.980 --> 00:34:26.820 <v PXA> Squeeze it and throw it in the waste basket.
00:34:26.820 --> 00:34:27.139 <v Edward Miller> Right.
00:34:27.139 --> 00:34:27.820 <v PXA> But it was safe.
00:34:27.820 --> 00:34:30.420 <v Edward Miller> And did twin twin tell you this?
00:34:30.420 --> 00:34:36.420 <v PXA> Some people– no. He didn't know about that. Yeah. And the other people would know about it. They told me about that.
00:34:36.420 --> 00:34:36.900 <v Edward Miller> I see.
00:34:36.900 --> 00:35:21.099 <v PXA> So I checked with [inaudible]. All right. That's true. But I would like to go there to talk to <c.287>Ngo Dinh Can</c> about that. So I asked my cousin. I mean, the chief of security there to introduce me and then that I would like to interview him, to write a story or write it. At that time, I worked for <c.288>Reuters</c>. Write about the coup d'état. And he is the man who was supposed to save the regime. It's very important. And you know about that. And I said, sure, but let me ask it first. So <c.289>Ngo Dinh Can</c> agreed to see me, you know, at least someone knows about that. Besides, he and his security and knew.
00:35:21.099 --> 00:35:21.860 <v Edward Miller> Right.
00:35:21.860 --> 00:35:32.780 <v PXA> Anyway, so he agreed to meet me. So very early in the morning, I was driven to his, you know, the fishing house. You know.
00:35:32.780 --> 00:35:33.340 <v Edward Miller> In <c.290>Huế</c>?
00:35:33.340 --> 00:35:44.539 <v PXA> In <c.291>Huế</c>, Cửa Thuận beach. Very beautiful house. Beautiful or not. We got up very early in the morning and ready to fish, et cetera.
00:35:44.539 --> 00:35:45.300 <v Edward Miller> I see.
00:35:45.300 --> 00:35:48.659 <v PXA> He enjoy life that way.
00:35:48.659 --> 00:35:51.420 <v Edward Miller> So this was right after the coup?
00:35:51.420 --> 00:35:52.703 <v PXA> After the coup about–
00:35:52.703 --> 00:35:54.000 <v Edward Miller> <c.292>1960</c>?
00:35:54.000 --> 00:35:56.000 <v PXA> After <c.293>1960</c>.
00:35:56.000 --> 00:35:57.000 <v Edward Miller> So <c.294>1961</c>?
00:35:57.000 --> 00:37:15.000 <v PXA> <c.295>'61</c> or something like that, yeah. <c.296>November '60</c> I went there, I think January or <c.297>December '60</c> or <c.298>'61</c>. I don't remember. But I wish to have a good story. And ask him about that, et cetera. He said yes, I did it, et cetera. So I want to know. The reason is because Mr. <c.299>Nhu</c> said that you don't know anything. Frankly speaking. You know, I'm suddenly–I'm very frank. I repeat what I heard And then Dr. <c.300>Tuyến</c> and many other people said that you don't know much. You just, you know, know only in <c.301>Huế</c> that's so. Yeah. But not much. And but what–my curiosity is, please tell me, how do you know about that? That's what I wish to know. He said: "Very simple. I arrested almost all the Communist agents in <c.302>Saigon</c>, including those sent from <c.303>North Vietnam</c>. See that? So I kidnapped them and took them to <c.304>Huế</c>. So my brother didn't know the security. He didn't know. I just kidnapped them. That's all very simple."
00:37:15.000 --> 00:37:20.489 <v Edward Miller> Right, but the coup was carried out by <c.305>VNQDD</c>, right?
00:37:20.489 --> 00:37:59.769 <v PXA> Yeah. By the other. So these are VCs. They have the duty to follow everything. Military? Not much. No military because fighting, but political activity. And they follow all the political parties in <c.306>the South</c> and religion. That's their assignment to follow them. Because for political struggling after the signing of the <c.307>Geneva Agreement</c>, <c.308>'54</c> to <c.309>'56</c> for election. And now, no election, et cetera.<c.310></c>
00:37:59.769 --> 00:38:04.409 <v PXA> See that? So they carry all kind of activity against the regime.
00:38:04.409 --> 00:38:05.409 <v Edward Miller> Right.
00:38:05.409 --> 00:38:29.809 <v PXA> So I realized with the American visa supported by the American and <c.311>SEATO</c>, et cetera, it takes very long, long time for the communists to take over. But our regime here, my brother regime, can be overthrown by these damn nationalists.
00:38:29.809 --> 00:38:31.090 <v Edward Miller> I see.
00:38:31.090 --> 00:39:43.760 <v PXA> Nationalist opposition. So to know them. Very simple. Like calling capture <c.312><c.313>VC</c></c> and North Vietnamese telling them to report– those who agree– to report their knowledge about the activity of the opposition, those who put the code, those who attempt code, et cetera. tell me I keep it secret. I wouldn't reveal your name or anything. I keep my promise. But after that, I released you and you agree. And then you continue your activity by following these people and then report to me secretly through our man, you know, without anyone knowing about that. So the communists don't know that you were captured either. You are there. So I–you told me. Can you ask a Catholic to step on the cross? No. No. Catholic. They had to step on the cross of Jesus Christ.
00:39:43.760 --> 00:39:44.760 <v Edward Miller> Right.
00:39:44.760 --> 00:39:56.000 <v PXA> So you ask the communists to fight against communists. Let's see. No sense, no use. They would lie or they would never tell you the truth.
00:39:56.000 --> 00:39:56.480 <v Edward Miller> Right.
00:39:56.480 --> 00:40:32.719 <v PXA> So you have the way to let them have the chance [you're not to work for us is to denounce] those who–the most immediate threat to the regime. So they report what they know about that, and what they heard about that. Then I ordered my men to follow these people to <c.314>Saigon</c>, here and etcetera, in the countryside. That's why I know that the coup is going to happen in the military people, thanks to the <c.315>VC</c> that I capture.
00:40:32.719 --> 00:40:36.320 <v Edward Miller> Because he was following them. He knew that the VC that were captured would not––<c.316></c>
00:40:36.320 --> 00:40:42.880 <v PXA> Their profession is to follow these people, and to push them to carry activity against the regime.
00:40:42.880 --> 00:40:47.960 <v Edward Miller> So the <c.317>VC</c> then had penetrated the <c.318>VNQDD</c> and the other groups
00:40:47.960 --> 00:41:26.070 <v PXA> Everyone, everywhere. So <c.319>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> is very smart. I said, all right, thank you very much. I will write a story about that, but not to go too detailed. "All right, but before you write, you let me know. You publish, you let me know." So I returned to <c.320>Saigon</c>. I talked to <c.321>Ngô Đình Nhu's</c> people. "You thought <c.322>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> is stupid. He's not stupid. He's smarter than you people!" He remembered by heart all the names, even the commander of the second Military Corps. General at that time–Colonel <c.323>Tôn Thất Đính</c>.Ngô Đình Nhu's people. "You thought <c.324>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> is stupid. He's not stupid. He's smarter than you people!" He remembered by heart all the names, even the commander of <c.325>the second Military Corps</c>. General–at that time, Colonel–<c.326>Tôn Thất Đính</c>.
00:41:26.070 --> 00:41:41.510 <v PXA> He said that is stupid. You know the Indigène Garde [<c.327>Garde Indigène</c>]. You know, khố xanh khố đỏ [blue and red belt]. [inaudi<c.328>bl</c>e] He recruited his people, he made them general, he made them colonel, et cetera.
00:41:41.510 --> 00:41:42.949 <v Edward Miller> So <c.329>Cẩn</c> recruited <c.330>Tôn Thất Đính</c>?
00:41:42.949 --> 00:42:16.150 <v PXA> Yeah, <c.331>Tôn Thất Đính</c> too! You look at it, he's so stupid! He confiscated the <c.332><c.333>FULRO</c></c>, you know, carry the activity, and some FULRO followed the VC. He ordered to confiscate everyth<c.334>ing, incl</c>uding the arrow and bow. How can they make a living? They should use it to kill the animal. You confiscate their weapon.
00:42:16.150 --> 00:42:18.829 <v Edward Miller> Who ordered this? This was <c.335>Cẩn</c>?
00:42:18.829 --> 00:42:21.710 <v PXA> Ngô Đình–<c.336>Tôn Thất Đính</c>!
00:42:21.710 --> 00:42:23.550 <v Edward Miller> <c.337>Tôn Thất Đính</c>, when he was in the <c.338>Highlands</c>?
00:42:23.550 --> 00:42:36.389 <v PXA> Yea, so <c.339>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> called him in and said you are stupid! You should return it to them, but you confiscate all the weapon. But that's why you had to return to it.
00:42:36.389 --> 00:42:41.789 <v Edward Miller> So<c.340> Ngô Đình Cẩn</c>, it seems, at least for a while, his strategies were very effective?
00:42:41.789 --> 00:42:42.630 <v PXA> Very effective.
00:42:42.630 --> 00:42:55.030 <v Edward Miller> And he was–he seems to have been less Catholic than his brothers, in the sense that he did not rely only on Catholics. He tried to win support of other groups.
00:42:55.030 --> 00:43:09.190 <v PXA> He tried to build constituency, because he carried secret activity under the French. His family actually worked together with <c.341>Ngô Đình Thục</c>.
00:43:09.190 --> 00:43:10.000 <v Edward Miller> With <c.342>Ngô Đình Thục</c>.
00:43:10.000 --> 00:43:36.869 <v PXA> <c.343>Ngô Đình Thục</c> was the leader of the family. And <c.344>Ngô Đình Thục</c> is a friend of [Francis] <c.345>Cardinal Spellman</c>. Both of them were promoted bishop at the same time by <c.346>Vatican</c>. The other one was Bishop of <c.347>New York</c>, while this one was Bishop of <c.348>Vĩnh Long</c>. The first bishop in <c.349>Vietnam</c>, and they were good friends. And you know, the P XII [<c.350>Pope Pius XII</c>], he worked for the American intelligence.
00:43:36.869 --> 00:43:38.070 <v Edward Miller> I'm sorry. Who?
00:43:38.070 --> 00:43:40.349 <v PXA> <c.351>The Pope</c>.
00:43:40.349 --> 00:43:41.070 <v Edward Miller> <c.352>The Pope</c>?
00:43:41.070 --> 00:44:19.980 <v PXA> He worked for the U.S. intelligence. And then he knows how to put these two guys together. That's why, under the directive of <c.353>Cardinal Spellman</c>, <c.354>Ngô Đình Thục</c> know how to get in touch with the Catholics, who saw the <c.355>Việt Minh</c> in the jungle, <c.357>inc</c>luding <c.356><c.358>Phạm Ngọc <c.359>Thảo</c></c></c>, the son of his friend, Adrian Phạm Ngọc Thuần. The father of Phạm Ngọc Thảo. So he told Adrian to tell Thảo if something interesting, just give me the report. So he did it.<c.360></c>
00:44:19.980 --> 00:44:20.539 <c.361>Thục</c>?
00:44:20.539 --> 00:44:24.579 <v PXA> This is <c.362>Thục</c> in Vĩnh Long.
00:44:24.579 --> 00:44:26.260 <v Edward Miller> And when did this happen?
00:44:26.260 --> 00:44:31.380 <v PXA> During the fight against the French. <c.363>Thảo</c> was in the jungle. He worked for the intelligence over there.
00:44:31.380 --> 00:44:37.300 <v Edward Miller> Okay, but that was the time that <c.364>Thục</c> started relationship with <c.365>Thảo</c>?
00:44:37.300 --> 00:44:39.340 <v PXA> That's right.
00:44:39.340 --> 00:45:51.889 <v PXA> Yeah, that's why–and many other stories. What I mean is <c.366>Ngô Đình Thục</c> and <c.367>Cardinal Spellman</c> knew each other a long time ago, and both of them work for the American authorities secretly against the French. You see the point there? Particularly when in <c.368>1950</c>, when the French lost too much money, et cetera, and their budget is too small. <c.369>The Expeditionary Corps</c> need a lot of supplies and someone to foot the bill; if not, they have to end the war. But the Americans have to continue the war because they have a planetary policy against <c.370>the Cold War</c>. That's why the American president agreed to foot the bill for <c.371>the French Expeditionary Corps</c>. That's why they signed the agreement in <c.372>1950</c>. And then with two conditions. This is–they call these two conditions come from the Wilson Doctrine.
00:45:51.889 --> 00:45:55.409 <v Edward Miller> I'm sorry. The Wilson Doctrine?
00:45:55.409 --> 00:46:29.170 <v PXA> Self determination for all the colonies. So that's the <c.373>World War One</c>, right after <c.374>Woodrow Wilson's Doctrine</c>, they call it self determination. So the American ask the French government, you have two things to do: Set up a Vietnamese government and set up the Vietnamese armed forces. And the French agreed, and then they sent a marshal–<c.375>de Lattre de Tassigny</c>–to do it.
00:46:29.170 --> 00:46:47.530 <v Edward Miller> Yeah. That's that's clear from the American documents that they're pushing the French in that regard. But if we could go back to <c.376>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> for a second and his relationship with with <c.377>Ngô Đình Thục</c>. So did you end up publishing that story?
00:46:47.530 --> 00:47:12.610 <v PXA> No, in the end, it wasn't very good. But please, the people mouth, very dangerous. We Vietnamese have a saying "The tongue has no bone, the mouth has no ring." So you can say different ways.
00:47:12.610 --> 00:47:14.650 <v Edward Miller> So you thought it was too dangerous for you?
00:47:14.650 --> 00:47:16.010 <v PXA> No, for him.
00:47:16.010 --> 00:47:18.730 <c.378><c.379>Cẩn</c></c> said–
00:47:18.730 --> 00:47:35.329 <v PXA> <c.380>Cẩn</c> said "Alright, good story, but please don't publish it for my sake." So I will give you another favor if you want to. I know you love animal, so I will give you any animal you like. But he likes me very much.
00:47:35.329 --> 00:47:51.202 <v Edward Miller> I see. Okay. What about after <c.381>1960</c>? In around the same time as the coup, <c.382>Ngô Đình Thục</c> became Archbishop of Huế.
00:47:51.202 --> 00:48:08.170 <v PXA> He wanted to be Archbishop here. But he got objection of the people, and particularly <c.383>Vatican</c>, so he dared not go too far. That's why they have here well known <c.384>Paul Nguyễn Văn Bình</c>.
00:48:08.170 --> 00:48:21.170 <v Edward Miller> Right? Right. And so <c.385>Thục</c> does not become <c.386>Archbishop of Saigon</c>, but becomes Archbishop of Huế. Does that mean that that <c.387>Cẩn</c>'s influence is reduced?
00:48:21.170 --> 00:49:03.559 <v PXA> No, not reduced. He worked grassroots. And then his problem was this: he shared with me [inaudible] entente. That means the understanding between <c.388>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> and <c.389>Nhu</c> and <c.390>Diệm</c>, because they know under their authority there's all kind of people: ministers, officials, officers, et cetera. Those were met <c.391>Cẩn</c> in Central Vietnam, they come and report to <c.392>Nhu</c>.
00:49:03.559 --> 00:49:04.480 <v Edward Miller> To <c.393>Nhu</c>?
00:49:04.480 --> 00:49:22.079 <v PXA> And those who met <c.394>Nhu</c>, they went to <c.395>Huế</c> to report to <c.396>Cẩn</c>. Right. So they make believe they were rivalry, in order to get the report of the disillusioned people working under them, in order to control them, to follow them in the future. So it's smart. They are so smart.
00:49:22.079 --> 00:49:27.320 <v Edward Miller> <c.397>Nhu</c> and <c.398>Cẩn</c> really didn't have a rivalry. They were just pretending?
00:49:27.320 --> 00:49:32.639 <v PXA> Like one throw the ball, the other one catch the ball.
00:49:32.639 --> 00:49:39.960 <v Edward Miller> Okay. And how did–
00:49:39.960 --> 00:49:51.800 <v PXA> But sometime he met––he loved animals, but because of because of the flatterer. The important thing is the sycophant is very dangerous.
00:49:51.800 --> 00:49:53.639 <v Edward Miller> The Catholics in <c.399>Central Vietnam</c>?
00:49:53.639 --> 00:50:19.920 <v PXA> Catholic or anyone. That's why you read The Prince<c.400> of Machiavel</c>li. He taught the prince how to avoid flatterer. So anyone you need advice, just ask. But if not anyone come to give you an idea; that one is a flatterer. That's why <c.401>Ngô Đình Cẩn</c> is very smart. He's much smarter than Nhu. He's much smart<c.403>er than</c> <c.402>Thục</c>.
00:50:19.920 --> 00:50:33.239 <v Edward Miller> Well if <c.404>Cẩn</c> had been so effective against the Đảng Cộng Sản up until the late <c.405>1950</c>’s–<c.406></c><c.407></c>
00:50:33.239 --> 00:50:46.590 <v PXA> You know, eighty-five percent out of sixty thousand killed or captured by the <c.408>Diệm</c> regime are mainly by <c.409>Ngô Ðình Cẩn</c> people.
00:50:46.590 --> 00:51:02.869 <v Edward Miller> Mainly by <c.410>Ngô Ðình Cẩn</c>. And if that was the case, why did it change after the <c.411>1950</c>’s? Because obviously the party makes a comeback and becomes much stronger. Why were <c.412>Cẩn</c>’s techniques no longer effective?
00:51:02.869 --> 00:51:43.429 <v PXA> <c.413>Cẩn</c>’s technique? He created animosity, he created hatred. Many of them joined the <c.414>Việt Minh</c> because they loved their country–they’re patriots, including the <c.415>Cao Đài</c>, <c.416>Hòa Hảo</c>, et cetera. They joined the <c.417>Việt Minh</c>, even t<c.420>he </c><c.418><c.419><c.422>Đại Việt</c></c></c>, too. Đại Việt, actually, was created by the <c.423>Japan</c>ese. It was <c.421>Komatsu</c> who created the Đại Việt. Komatsu, he was Deputy Chief of Counter Role institute in Japan. He also control <c.424>Trần Văn Chương</c>–
00:51:43.429 --> 00:51:45.161 <v Edward Miller> Oh, really?
00:51:45.161 --> 00:51:47.584 <v PXA> Yeah. The father of–
00:51:47.584 --> 00:51:48.994 <c.425>Trần Lệ Xuân</c>.
00:51:48.994 --> 00:52:15.309 <v PXA> <c.426>Trần Lệ Xuân</c> and <c.427>Trần Văn Thông</c>, the family under control of Komatsu. And when the Americans return, they used him, so he gave reports all of Đại Việt to the Americans. And Amer<c.428>icans recru</c>it them, and accept. When the French return, <c.429>1945</c>, they know how to use the <c.430><c.431>Đại Việt</c></c>, too. That’s why the Đại Việt is divided...those who work for the French, or those who work for the Americans, et cetera.<c.432></c><c.433></c>
00:52:15.309 --> 00:52:28.230 <v Edward Miller> But my question is, why is it if <c.434>Ngô Ðình Cẩn</c> is so effective against the party, and the party is really weakened–
00:52:28.230 --> 00:52:32.309 <v PXA> Oh, they very weakened, especially in <c.435>Central Vietnam</c>, very, very tough.
00:52:32.309 --> 00:52:41.630 <v Edward Miller> Why does the situation change? Because it changes it seems to me very quickly—<c.436>1959</c>, <c.437>1960</c>, <c.438>'61</c>—the party comes back and becomes much stronger.
00:52:41.630 --> 00:55:43.010 <v PXA> Yeah<c.439>, that’s</c> right. Actually, because of the people. <c.440>Ngô Ðình Diệm</c>'s regime has no constituency. In <c.441>Vietnam</c>, you should use at least one constituency, either the army…in the past, under the French, or the French Army, the Vietnamese were suppletif [auxillary] force, you know, not a real army. But under <c.442>Diệm</c>, it’s different. With the American money, they build things very fast. But the main thing is the people. You have a mandarin from <c.443>Huế</c> who control <c.444>everything.</c> And then the family control everything, and they do not allow even loyal opposition, like those who fought against the <c.445>Việt Minh</c>. They were kicked out and outlawed, too. Many of them were captured and killed, too. So all of them gang together, that’s a one. The peasant, the peasant rely on what? On the land. And the land was confiscated. Because they were dispossessed, they were sent into first, the Agroville in <c.446>1960</c>. When I reported first to Dr. <c.447>Tuyến</c>, the Agroville were not appreciated, so he start over, to set up the Strategic Hamlet Program, the same thing but smaller size. And so they were disposed of, dispossessed of their land and their ancestral village. They had to go into the Agroville to live and to go outside five, ten kilometers by sampan to grow rice, et cetera. They just separate them from the Communist cadres. But when they go there, the Communists are still there, you see it, because they listen to the Chinese, because the Communist slogan is this: "The cadre and the people are like the water and the fish." So, if you just take out the water, the fish die. But you take out the water, the fish follow the water and go inside. So, that's why. The second important thing: in <c.448><c.451><c.452>Vietnam</c></c></c>, they had a village election that the French respected and <c.449>Ngô Ðình Diệm</c> get rid of it in <c.450>1956</c>. And another law, any Chinese or foreigner living in Vietnam, born in Vietnam, should take Vietnamese–
00:55:43.010 --> 00:55:44.369 <v Edward Miller> Nationality.
00:55:44.369 --> 00:56:33.050 <v PXA> Citizenship. Those who don’t want to do it, just out of the government and no business, et cetera. It’s difficult. Only one who dare to oppose, he so proud of himself, and you know his name, <c.453><c.454>Nguyễn Văn Điềm</c></c>, engineer. Mr. Nguyễn Văn Điềm, engineer. He speak French, he prefer to speak French better than Vietnamese; he speak English very well, too. And then he’s Director-General of Planning for <c.455><c.456>Diệm</c></c>, when Diệm became president, et cetera, for very long time. Those work for him are very well-known too, including <c.457>Vũ Văn Thái</c>. The one who works with–
00:56:33.050 --> 00:56:35.489 <v<c.458> Edward </c>Miller> He's director of the Office of Foreign Aid.
00:56:35.489 --> 00:56:42.329 <v PXA> Yeah, and then he work with the one who get the <c.459>Pentagon</c> paper and leak out–
00:56:42.329 --> 00:56:43.130 <v Edward Miller> <c.460>Ellsberg</c>.<c.461></c>
00:56:43.130 --> 00:58:01.530 <v PXA> Ellsberg! Afterwards he work for the <c.462>U.N.</c> or something like that, <c.463>Vũ Văn Thái</c>. So, that man, the rest of them, have to take Vietnamese citizenship in order to continue business. So he create more and more animo<c.464>sity, m</c>ore enemy intellectual. He could not get the intelligent to support him. All the intellectuals who would like to have, you call it, profiter, opportunist. He had to have position in the army, in the government, in business, et cetera, but in very small circles. So those on the outside hate these people, you see it? So the only way to them is to give support to the <c.465>V.C.</c> or the <c.466><c.467>Việt Minh</c></c>, particularly the Việt Minh. They don’t know much about Communism because the Communists very smart: they never talk Communism. Even now, for instance, they talk about Communism, but they don’t follow it. When they took over the government according to the teaching of <c.468>Marx</c>, you know what happen? The government fades out.
00:58:01.530 --> 00:58:04.570 <v Edward Miller> Right, the government would whither away.
00:58:04.570 --> 00:58:37.480 <v PXA> Whither away! We translate in Vietnamese “Tiêu vong,” that mean “die”—more serious. But ask the Communist party, they die only when they are overthrown by the people or when they have implosion like <c.469>the Soviet Union</c>. So if you ask the cadre, particularly the politician, when you take over the government, "How about that one? Why you continue all the time, when you whither out?" And then they refuse to answer.
00:58:37.480 --> 00:58:45.719 <v Edward Miller> I see. So let me ask you about–
00:58:45.719 --> 00:59:09.719 <v PXA> So <c.470>Ngô Ðình Cẩn</c>, I went there. See, I give you some anecdote, many anecdote. He like a cow, with a cow milk. So, the people in <c.471>Saigon</c>, particular people in <c.472>Huế</c>, know that he like cow milk, fresh milk. But they have <c.473><c.474>Bến Cát</c></c> here, you know Bến Cát Dairy farm?
00:59:09.719 --> 00:59:11.079 <v Edward Miller> Oh <c.475>Bến Cát</c>.<c.476></c>
00:59:11.079 --> 00:59:45.239 <v PXA> Run by <c.477>Mr. Carter</c>, he was Colonel, he was Colonel during <c.478>World War II</c>.
